content.title: Review
content.review:
Summary

This paper studies the loss surface of complex-valued neural networks with quadratic activation and (complex-)ReLU activation functions. This paper shows that in case of 1-hidden-layer complex neural networks with quadratic activation functions, there is no bad local minimum in the training loss. In contrast, complex ReLU networks are shown to have bad local minima.

Strength

This paper studies the optimization landscape of complex-valued neural networks, which has not received much attention in the literature. The paper extends results by (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2019) and (Yun et al., 2019) to shallow complex-valued networks and obtains similar results as the real-valued counterparts. The paper gives a good literature overview of complex-valued neural networks, and also a good review on calculus of complex variables.

Weakness
- The paper considers the setting where only the first layer of the network is optimized, while the parameters in the second layer are fixed. I am skeptical whether the positive result on quadratic activation can be extended to deeper networks.
- I believe the proofs given in the paper are not self-contained. In the beginning of the paper the authors emphasize that the difference of real vs complex variables can result in nontrivial differences in the loss landscape. However, when it comes to proofs, the paper carelessly states “the rest of the proof can be done in the same way as the real-valued networks”, without fully addressing the potential issues in extending real variables to complex variables. To be more specific, at the end of page 7, the paper says “the proof of the first case is the same as in (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2019)” without even pointing out which part of the cited paper should be looked at. Also, the proof of Theorem 2 (on complex-ReLU activation) ends abruptly by saying “the rest of the proof follows as in (Yun et al., 2019)”.
- In Section 1.1.2, the authors claim that Assumption C in (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2019) is restrictive and unrealistic. However, given that we have the freedom to choose the second layer parameters $v$, I am not fully convinced that this assumption is necessarily strong or unrealistic. Also, although I didn’t find it stated anywhere, it seems to me from Section 3.3 that Theorem 1 of this paper also implicitly assumes $k \geq d$, which is not much different from the requirement $k \geq 2d$ in Assumption C (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2019) because the network is complex-valued. The reason why I believe Theorem 1 assumes $k \geq d$ is that the proof considers a case "${\rm rank}(D_v W) = d$,” which can hold only if $k \geq d$. This makes me think that both theorems are rather direct extensions of the real-valued counterparts, without providing any interesting difference between complex vs real neural networks. Please do correct me if I’m mistaken.

Overall Assessment

Although this paper brings up an interesting problem to look at, due to the weaknesses pointed out above, I believe the paper does not meet the standard for acceptance.

Minor comments
- Some uses of \citep should be replaced with \citet, e.g. in Section 1.1.1.
- At the end of Section 1.1.2, it is stated that “non-linear neural networks can approximate any function by universal approximation theorem.” However, if we are considering 1-hidden-layer networks, just non-linearity is not enough; the activation must be non-polynomial. For example, if the activation function is quadratic, the network can only represent quadratic functions of the input, so one can never approximate higher order polynomials.
- Section 3.1.1, 2nd derivative w.r.t. $w_p$: missing $\partial$ in the denominator.
- Lemma 2: shouldn’t $h$ be a $kd$-dimensional vector instead of a matrix?
- In Section 3.3, the matrix $U$ comes out of nowhere, without any explanation.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
We appreciate your kind feedbacks and the time devoted to reading our paper. Since all your concerns are technical, we would like to illustrate that all the concerns mentioned in your comments can be clarified. 

First of all, there is a big misunderstanding where you thought the unrealistic assumption in (Soltanolkotabi et al., 2019) is $k>2d$, which makes our work seems to be just an extension. In fact, they ***set the weights of the output layer v so as to have at least d positive entries and at least d negative entries*** (Please see the statement of Theorem 2.1 on Page 3 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.04926.pdf). It is an extremely unrealistic assumption and their proof is mainly based on this unrealistic assumption (Page 19 in their paper). It is very unrealistic because there is no way to ensure a neural net will have ***at least d positive weights and at least d negative weights*** during and after training, especially with algorithm like backprop. We totally avoided this unrealistic assumption. Therefore our paper is not an extension of their result and that is why we have a very different proof. The novelty of our "no unrealistic assumption" result is a key contribution of our work, which makes a stark distinction between all previous works and ours. We apologize that if we have stated it more clearly then there would be no such a misunderstanding. Besides, we don't think the assumption of $k>2d$ is unrealistic (will discuss more later).

Now we would like to respond the three weakness points and minor comments in your feedback one by one.

- (first weakness point):
The result of our paper will be the same if v is not fixed and that's is another benefit of using complex-valued weights. Let W be the first weight matrix and v be the second weight vector. The second layer is fixed because a global minimum w.r.t. W is also a global minimum w.r.t. (W, v). Therefore optimizing both W and v is the same as optimizing only W. For example, if $v \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is fixed to be (1,1,1), and a (2, -3i, 999 - 7i) is needed for achieving global minimum, then we just multiply the first row of W by $\sqrt{2}$, multiply the second row of W by $\sqrt{-3i}$, and multiply the third row of W by $\sqrt{999 - 7i}$. The final W together with (1,1,1) is the same as the another W together with (2, -3i, 999 - 7i). Therefore fixing v and optimizing only W will be enough. Complex-valued weights make quadratic no longer maps just to positive numbers, which makes the optimization landscape superior. Therefore we conjecture that the result holds for deeper networks as well.

- (second weakness point):
Yes, complex and real variables can be very different but since complex numbers and real numbers are both *field* there is still a lot in common. We indeed have two places saying “the rest of the proof can be done in the same way as the real-valued networks” but we have carefully verified it is true. We have explained why there will not be potential issues in extending real variables to complex variables in the new version we uploaded. For the first place in proving theorem 1, the omitted part is just multiplying a matrix by it's left inverse. Multiplying a matrix by it's left inverse is the same in both complex and real cases. We have added the full proof of the omitted part in the new version. For the second place in the end of proving theorem 2, the rest proof is exactly the same as in the previous paper because we assumed our input dataset to be real-valued (the neural net is still complex-valued). The omitted part is just to construct a point that has lower loss and ***there is no need to extend their proof to the complex-valued case***. We now provided a sketch proof at the end. More explanations can be founded in our newly uploaded paper.

- (third weakness point):
We have addressed your main concern at the beginning. One more thing to clarify. Yes we indeed need $k \geq d$ (thank you for pointing it out) and we have added it on our new version. However, since over-parametrization is so common in deep learning, having a larger number of hidden nodes than the number of input nodes is quite realistic and it is almost everywhere in practice.

- (minor comments):
Thank you for the typos you pointed out. We have uploaded a new version where the typos are fixed.
We do not understand what do you mean by "if the activation function is quadratic, the network can only represent quadratic functions of the input". If we have a 1-hidden-layer network but with a large number of hidden nodes in the layer, quadratic activated neural networks can still approximate any function. Many paper studied the fact that with nonlinearity and enough hidden nodes, shallow networks can approximate any function.
$\bf{h} = \text{vec}(\bf{U})$ as in the proof of Lemma 2. We have added it in the new version. Thank you so much.

We would like to thank you again for your nice review and we are sorry about the places that we did not state clearly previously.

content.title: Still not convinced
content.comment:
Thank you very much for the response, but I am still not convinced with some of the points that the authors make, including:

- Assumption C: I do agree to the authors that there is no way to ensure a neural net will have at least d positive weights and at least d negative weights *during and after training*. However, Theorem 2.1 of the cited paper considers the case where only $W$ is considered as parameters to optimize, and $v$ remains *fixed* over training. Thus, putting $d$ +1's and $d$ -1's to $v$ is sufficient, so I don't see anything "unrealistic" about it, and I'm not still convinced that this paper provides so different a result than the real NN one.

- I'm convinced with the authors' intuition that there may still be no bad local minima even when both $W$ and $v$ are optimized. In fact, I believe that if you can show an example of spurious local minima for 2-layer real quadratic NNs (when both layers are optimized) and also non-existence of spurious local minima for 2-layer complex quadratic NN (again, both layers optimized), this will be a very nice result that makes complex NNs really stand out. However, at the current status of the manuscript, only $W$ is optimized with $v$ fixed, which I believe is essentially the same as the real NN result (up to a factor of 2 in width); so I believe the paper falls short of showing the advantage of complex NNs.

- Universal approximation theorem: In a 2-layer quadratic network $f(x) = \sum_i v_i \phi (w_i^T x)$, where $\phi: x \mapsto x^2$, the network boils down to $f(x) = x^T (\sum_i v_i w_i w_i^T) x$ which is a quadratic function, so universal approximation theorem cannot hold. See also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_approximation_theorem. My point was that the activation $\phi$ has to be *nonpolynomial* if universal approximation theorem were to hold.

content.title: Thank you for your feedbacks!
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedbacks and we understand your arguements. 

Firstly we do not require v to have at least d positive and d negative entries. Our v can be arbitrary. We believe that is a stark distinction between real and complex networks. We agree with you that 

"In fact, I believe that if you can show an example of spurious local minima for 2-layer real quadratic NNs (when both layers are optimized) and also non-existence of spurious local minima for 2-layer complex quadratic NN (again, both layers optimized), this will be a very nice result that makes complex NNs really stand out."

For the first result of "spurious local minima for 2-layer real quadratic NNs (when both layers are optimized)" is already shown on the paper "SMALL NONLINEARITIES IN ACTIVATION FUNCTIONS CREATE BAD LOCAL MINIMA IN NEURAL NETWORKS". That is Theorem 2 on page 6. (Also check their Corollary 3 on page 7).

For the second result of "non-existence of spurious local minima for 2-layer complex quadratic NN (again, both layers optimized)", we believe it is not hard to be proved. We will try to have this result ASAP before Nov.24 and update it to our draft. We will let you know once the draft is updated with the proof. Thank you very much for your comments! We really appreciate that. So stay tuned.

content.title: Interesting result, proof clarifications will help
content.review:
### Summary:

This paper is theoretical and aims to prove a theorem stating that no spurious local minima exist for one hidden layer complex-valued networks with a quadratic activation. This is done without unrealistic assumptions. The bulk of the literature focuses on real-valued networks and given the already demonstrated potential of complex-valued networks it makes sense to perform such analysis for complex-valued networks. Wirtinger calculus and related technical tools are used to obtain derivatives for complex-valued functions. The proof is inspired by Soltanolkotabi et al. 2019 who prove the same result for real-valued networks of the same structure (with assumptions). 

The paper also introduces another theorem for similar structured networks with a complex-ReLU instead. The way the paper is written, it is not the main focus of the paper. The proof for this follows Yun et al. 2019. 


########################################

### Strong points:

The paper is well motivated and the authors convey the importance of the problem. Furthermore, required knowledge such as Wirtinger calculus is explained with care.

The result that there are no spurious local minima is interesting.

Unlike previous similar results (mainly for real-valued networks), the proven theorem with quadratic activations does not have any assumptions that are unrealistic. 


########################################

### Weak points:

In Lemma 2 the defined matrix, $\tilde{\nabla}^2 \mathcal{L}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}})$, is not the Hessian (compare to the Hessian at the bottom of page 5). However, the proof of Lemma 2 uses this matrix as a Hessian in order to do a second order expansion. Why was $\tilde{\nabla}^2 \mathcal{L}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}})$ defined in this way? If the actual Hessian is used, it should still be possible to show that the quantity is real. 
[Note that actually the order of the derivatives in $\tilde{\nabla}^2 \mathcal{G}_i (\tilde{\mathbf{W}})$ in the proof is not the same as the order of the derivatives in $\tilde{\nabla}^2 \mathcal{L}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}})$ of Lemma 2. This should be corrected]

Lemma 2 states that it hold for *all* complex-valued $\mathbf{h}$. However, the last step of the proof of Lemma 2 states that $\|\|\mathbf{h}\|\|$ should be ‘small enough’. How does this let the lemma hold for all $\mathbf{h}$? Furthermore, how come the final inequality in the proof of Lemma 2 is guaranteed to always hold by truncating the series expansion and ignoring higher order terms?

Please can the authors explain the final steps starting from the proof by contradiction step in the proof of Theorem 1 in more detail? It is mentioned that $(b_1, b_2)$ can be chosen depending on $(a_1, a_2)$. However, after $\mathcal{M}$ is defined, $\mathbf{b}$ is being designed without any consideration for $(a_1, a_2)$. It seems that we need to guarantee that $(b_1, b_2)$ obeys certain values depending on $(a_1, a_2)$---for example when $a_1 >0$, $a_2 <0$ we do not want $b_1 < 0$, $b_2 < 0$.

This work is a theoretical contribution and should be mainly viewed from that perspective. However, simple simulations verifying whether Theorem 1 holds would strengthen the paper. For example, using Wirtinger gradient descent, can the same loss function value be obtained using different random initialization points? As Soltanolkotabi et al. 2019 considers a similar network structure, simulations showing that their assumptions are indeed not required in complex-valued networks would also help.


########################################

### Recommendation:

Overall I lean towards rejection. I think the result that there are no spurious local minima with no assumptions is interesting, however, there are some questions regarding some of the proofs which should be clarified.


########################################

### Additional questions and clarifications that will help assessment:

Please address and clarify my above questions and queries.

It would be useful to describe the proof strategy and high level steps for the proof of Theorem 1 before proceeding with the proof. Furthermore as some of the proof is similar to Soltanolkotabi et al. 2019, it would help if the differences and novelties in the proof presented are highlighted.

The proof for Theorem 2 is tricky to follow because it appears to prove a more general result and multiple new quantities are introduced. It would be helpful to connect back to the statement of the theorem more. Furthermore, while it is following Yun et al 2019, it would be useful to explain the high level methodology in more detail. As a reader who is not familiar with their original proof this would be invaluable.


########################################

### Additional feedback that does not necessarily impact recommendation:

There is a typo with the vectors in the Taylor expansion in the proof of Lemma 2. For example the first order term has a dot product with $\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{h} \\\\ \mathbf{h} \end{pmatrix} $

Should the final sentence of Lemma 2 be $\mathbf{h} \in \mathbb{C}^{kd}$ because $\mathbf{h}$ is a vector?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
We appreciate your kind feedbacks and the time devoted to reading our paper. Since all your concerns are technical, we would like to illustrate that all the concerns mentioned in your comments can be clarified.

-(Weak points):
- It is a typo which does not affect the whole analysis. We have fixed it in the newly uploaded version. Swapping the two diagonal terms is enough to fix it. Thank you for pointing it out.
- It is actually a standard proof of “hessian matrix is semi-positive definite if the variable is a local minimum”. The second half of our proof ( where you questioned about ) is exactly the same as a standard proof for real-valued case. Many proofs can be found online and in textbooks. Intuitively speaking, higher order terms are ignored because they vanish much quicker. And a “small enough” neighborhood does not affect the result for “all h“ because essentially you could multiply a scalar at the end of both sides of the equation. Even if it is just a small neighborhood, our proof still hold true because the only thing we want is the “sign” of the complex vector $\textbf{b}$ but not the magnitude. 
- Since $\textbf{h} = \text{vect}(\textbf{U})$ is an arbitrary direction, and $\textbf{U} = \textbf{a}\textbf{b}^T$. By design we let $\textbf{a}$ from a null space therefore it is somewhat “fixed”. However, since $U$ is arbitrary, $\textbf{b}$ can be arbitrary. Thus, $\textbf{b}$ can be any complex vector we want. Since $\textbf{a}$ is “fixed”, $(a_1, a_2)$ is “fixed”. But since we can choose any $\textbf{b}$ we want, we can have any (b_1, b_2) we want. In conclusion, (a_1, a_2) does not decide (b_1, b_2), but “our will“ decides (b_1, b_2). Our will is to have a (b_1, b_2) so that we can make $\mathcal{H} = \frac{1}{2n}(a_1b_1 - a_2b_2) < 0$ to arrive a contradiction we want. If it is still unclear please let us know.
- We did not do an experiment because we planned to write this paper as a theoretical one. We believe an empirical experiment could be helpful. We might add this part in the future if we have a chance. 

-(Additional questions and clarifications that will help assessment):
- We have added a part to the newly uploaded version to illustrate your two suggestions. We copy and paste that part here. To prove Theorem 1 we make use of the semi-definite property of the Wirtinger hessian matrix. We will show that a local minimum $\textbf{W}$ must satisfy the expression in Lemma 3 which makes it to be a global minimum. The first half of the proof is similar to the proof of Theorem 2.1 in \citep{SJL19}. We derive a nice and simple expression of the hessian multiplied by an arbitrary direction $\textbf{U}$. Wirtinger calculus is used to extend their steps to the complex case. The second half of the proof turns out to be very different because we avoided their main assumption that $\textbf{v}$ having at least $d$ positive entries and at least $d$ negative entries, which is unrealistic. By using the property of complex numbers, we can show that a local minimum $\textbf{W}$ must satisfy the expression in Lemma 3 by contradiction. 
- We provided a sketch proof of the omitted part of Theorem 2. Please check out our newly uploaded version. The connection between $h(z)$ and $\mathbb{C}ReLU$ is that by setting $s_+ = 1$ and $s_- = 0$ in $h(z)$, $h(z)$ then becomes $\mathbb{C}ReLU$. 

-(Additional feedback that does not necessarily impact recommendation):
- Thank you very much. We have fixed this typo.

We would like to thank you again for your nice review and we are sorry about the places that we did not state clearly previously.

content.title: Response to author response
content.comment:
Thanks for addressing my queries.

I have understood and am now OK with the reasoning used in the proof for Lemma 2. I suggest adding similar explanations (or the reference if it is standard) to the proof to avoid similar confusion for other readers. Additionally the typos I mentioned are still not corrected in the Taylor expansion (top of page 14) as far as I can see… For example, why is the first order term multiplied by $\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{h} \\\\ \mathbf{h} \end{pmatrix}$? Shouldn’t it be $\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{h} \\\\ \mathbf{h^C} \end{pmatrix}$ (as shown at the top of page 6)? 

On a related note, why is the Hessian at the top of page 6 different to the Hessian used in Lemma 2 to do the second order expansion? For example, the top left term in the matrix of Lemma 2 should be $\nabla^2_{\mathbf{W}}\mathcal{L}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}})$ according to the Hessian on the top of page 6.

Thanks, I understand the ending of the proof of Theorem 1. Again I feel the presentation could be improved---some specific cases of the nonzero elements of $\mathcal{M}$ are described and a few sentences explaining how this covers any $\mathcal{M}$ would have helped.

I still feel the proof of theorem 2 is difficult to parse and lacks explanations for the various steps. It is also using more general expressions to be more like Yun et al. without a clear motivation and link to the main text of this paper…for example, there are multiple new quantities which are not related to the main text ($\mathbf{W}_1$, $\mathbf{W}_2$, $\mathbf{b}_1$, $\mathbf{b}_2$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\mathbf{u}$) and the reader is assumed to know them.

content.title: The authors prove the lack of local minima in a specific CVNN, but the generality and of this result is not clear.
content.review:
In the present work, the authors focus on a fairly specific type of complex valued neural network and prove that with analytic activation function the optimization landscape has no spurious local minima. On the other hand, when the activation is not analytic, e.g. with Crelu activation, local minima can appear in the landscape.
Personally, I found the polemic tone of the paper a bit unmotivated and the clarity of presentation a bit lacking. Describing all previous theoretical work on the subject as full of unrealistic assumptions (the detailed table is hard to read and referencing to external work seems to be necessary in order to understand it) and then taking a very specific example of a CVNN as the unbiased solution is slightly confusing. While many readers and practitioners may be unfamiliar with Wirtinger calculus, I think the basic crash course shouldn't appear in the main text of a conference paper.
I am not confident in believing that the presented study case can be really held as proof of superiority of CVNN to usual DNN, since the generality of the arguments used by the authors is not clear. Moreover, in practice optimization is usually not at all a problem for DNN and the focus is on generalization (not discussed here), so I don't think this work provides a strong reason for moving to CVNN as claimed by the authors.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedbacks.

- Generality. You mentioned it is a fairly specific type of complex valued neural network but in fact a large number of works have focused on quadratic activated neural networks. Except for the papers from TIT and NIPS we cited in our work, the best paper of COLT 2018 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.09203.pdf) is also about quadratic activated networks. And that's just to name a few. Moreover, analyzing shallow neural networks in so common in theoretical deep learning literature and shallow networks can actually be used in real-world problems. Apart from quadratic activations and being shallow, there is no other “restrictions”. More importantly, there is no unrealistic assumptions being made. Therefore we believe the generality of our work is well addressed. Analyzing quadratic networks is just the first step towards analyzing more practical networks like tanh activated networks. Since both quadratic and tanh functions are analytic we believe our result can be further extended to more general settings in the future.
- Polemic tone. There is a long line of work analyzing the global optimality of neural networks. An important direction of the work is to make unrealistic assumptions and then derive a specific type of neural network without poor local minima. Existence of such assumptions make their results not practical. The novelty of our "no unrealistic assumption" result is a key contribution of our work, which makes a stark distinction between all previous works and ours. We stated that neural networks with analytic activations could have no spurious local minima but with non-analytic activations could have many spurious local minima to emphasize the importance of analyticity. By comparing our Theorem 1 with Theorem 2, we can see that it is promising to study more complex-valued networks with analytic activations. Complex-valued neural networks have the potential to be deep non-linear neural networks with practical activations having no spurious local minima. Such result would be invaluable in modern deep learning era because existence of poor local minima is one of the most intractable problems in deep learning due to the non-convexity in optimization of neural networks.
- Generalization vs. Optimization. We believe both generalization and optimization are important topics in neural network ( along with many other topics like representation power ). In fact optimization is being paid more attention than generalization in recent years. ( You may count the number of papers being published on top conferences on these two topics. ) Since non-convexity in optimization of neural networks is extremely challenging, most cutting-edge researchers in deep learning theory are focusing on the optimization of neural nets. Sanjeev Arora, Tengyu Ma, Jason D. Lee, Chi Jin, Simon S. Du, and that's just to name a few. As for the generalization of complex-valued networks you mentioned, we believe it is not an important topic because essentially CVNNs can be expressed as two real-valued networks when we want to analyze its generalization capacity using methods like VC-dimension, Rademacher complexity and etc. All current generalization bounds can be applied to CVNNs trivially from RVNNs. Moreover, as we mentioned in our paper, there is one paper studied the generalization of CVNNs empirically and they found CVNNs have a better generalization ability compared to bi-real-valued neural networks.

Please let us know if there is anything still unclear to you. Thank you very much.
